newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan to keep easy credit despite U.S rate hike.
newsitem.headline: Japan to keep easy credit despite U.S rate hike.

text.p: Bank of Japan (BOJ) governor Yasuo Matsushita gave an upbeat assessment on Wednesday of the country's economy and ruled out a change in its easy credit policies.

Unruffled by the first U.S. hike in key rates for more than two years, Matsushita said Japan's priority was to keep its eyes on its own recovering economy which he said was becoming "Our monetary policy for now is to make the basis for economic recovery more solid, while keeping a close watch over financial and economic developments," he told a news conference.

Asked whether the U.S. Federal Reserve rate rise would affect Japan's monetary policy, Matsushita said: "Each nation sets its monetary policy by appropriately judging its domestic economic conditions."
He added that rather than reacting to a particular policy change by another nation, it was important to monitor the effect that the change has on Japan's economy.

The BOJ has kept the official discount rate that it charges banks at a record low of 0.5 percent since September 1995 to help economic recovery and to facilitate Japanese banks' disposal of problem loans.
At the same time, the central bank has been managing market liquidity to keep the key call rate below the discount rate on average since September 1995.

In its rate hike on Tuesday, the Fed increased its target for the federal funds rate that commercial banks charge each other for overnight loans to 5.50 percent from 5.25 percent in an effort to stay a step ahead of inflation. It left the discount rate unchanged at 5.0 percent.
Inflation risks are seen as limited in Japan as the stall in the yen's weakness and a drop in crude oil prices are unlikely to send prices of imported goods sky-rocketting, Matsushita said.

He said with a rise in the sales tax to five percent from the current three percent in April, it was inevitable that the economy will slow down temporarily, although the underlying economic recovery trend will continue.
The short-term effect of the tax hike, which will boost demand ahead of implementation and dampen demand afterwards, is likely to be mild, he said.
Prospects for the economy are bright with the strength in the private sector making up for dwindling support from the public sector.
A favourable economic cycle is at work in which higher output leads to better corporate profits and private consumption, and thus back to boosting production, he said.
"This is very encouraging when looking at future prospects," Matsushita said.
